notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1381.tmp1381.opp-lat: Scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'volantatem', 'por', 'Es quo', 'ex en'). 'vetuli nos' read as 'velut nos'. 'symponum' is probably a corruption of a Greek title for secretary or scribe; the rendering is uncertain. The opening parenthesis '(Timor ergo...' is never closed in the text. Several sentences are syntactically loose, and their sense is approximate: 'per commutationem summam redditionem', 'eum divinam praecessisse voluntatem', 'totum fateamur ab omni peccato Deum liberum esse', 'secundum utrumque', 'pro uno frustra omnia gerere'. The edition's own corrections are kept in brackets.

Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. pictatis = pietatis, praecidet = praesidet, vecabulum = vocabulum). 'superruam' read as 'superfluam'. 'hac idacque' is corrupt; rendered as 'for this reason' (hac de causa?), uncertain. 'compositiores inju(??)tas' read as 'compositiones injustas', uncertain. 'is(??)i ... fortissimi hanc fecerim' is garbled; read as 'ipsi ... fecerint'. 'almificum nomine' read as 'almificum nominent'. 'sine successu receptionem' is obscure; rendered literally. The emperor referred to is presumably Heraclius, and the predecessor/successor pair Sergius and Pyrrhus.

Line 11: 'Ecclesiasticam scripturae ... historiam' is read as 'scripturo' (dative, 'to you about to write'). The 'summa veritate docente' clause is obscure; rendered literally. 'usque ad praelationem tantummodo canonum' (Gregory on Chalcedon) is unclear; the sense seems to be that the synod was to be received except for its canons. The Scripture references are misprinted in the edition: they should be Luke 6:37, Lev. 19:14, Rom. 14:12–13. They are given as printed. The final sentence of line 11 breaks off mid-quotation (1 Sam. 16:7).

Line 13: 'liquid(??)' and 'dicta(??)as' read as 'liquido' and 'dictatas'. The apse verses (S. Agnese) are textually corrupt in this printing: 'nibeis' read as 'niveis'; 'ruribus' probably for 'roribus' (dew); 'irim' for 'irin' (rainbow), with the construction of lines 19–20 unclear; 'Sursum versa nutu' and 'Vestibus et factis' are obscure and translated tentatively. The heading 'Epitaph' is the edition's; the verses are a dedicatory apse inscription.

nodes.text: APPENDIX.
I.
EXTRACT FROM THE LETTER OF SAINT MAXIMUS TO MARINUS THE PRIEST, WHO MAKES, AMONG OTHER THINGS, A DEFENCE FOR HONORIUS.
(Mansi, Conc. Collect., vol. XII.)

I think that Honorius, the Roman pope, too, does not deny the natural duality of wills in Christ in the letter he wrote to Sergius, by having said 'one will'; rather he confesses it, and perhaps even establishes it. For he did not say this in rejection of the human and natural will of the Saviour, but [to say] that in no way did the will of the flesh, or any vicious thought, precede his conception, which was without seed, or his incorrupt birth. For the divine and paternal will alone, through the only-begotten Son working by himself, brought about his own incarnation and this concurrence of the Holy Spirit; and that he follows this sense is clear from this. For when he had said that, because of the ineffable union of the human and divine nature, God is both said to suffer, and the humanity to have come down from heaven with the humanity [read: divinity], and had in this way shown the supreme exchange, by communication, of the things that are naturally present in each nature of the one Christ and Son of God, he adds: 'Whence', he says, 'we also confess one will of the Lord Jesus Christ,' in the way he says: 'Because indeed it was our nature that was assumed by the divinity, not [our] guilt,' that is, not [something] from sin, speaking almost together with the great Athanasius, who writes these things against the impious Apollinarius: 'He was born of a woman, raising up for himself the form of man from the first moulding, in the showing of the flesh without carnal wills and human thoughts, in the image of newness. For the will is of the divinity alone, since the whole nature is of the divinity. Thus the progress of the birth of the Word according to the flesh for our sake came about above us. For no vicious will or thought of the flesh preceded, as is seen in us, because of the desire for generation, which it acquired from the deception of the first parent; but the will of the divinity alone, through the Son, who according to the good pleasure of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit wrought, as I said, his own incorporation by himself, bearing in himself and through himself the newly devised mode of nature's birth, and accomplishing his own conception without seed from the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary.' So, having considered this ineffable manner of his birth, the one [Athanasius] said there was in him the will of the divinity alone, while this one [Honorius] said one will of our Lord Jesus Christ. 'Because indeed', he says, 'our nature, not [our] guilt, was assumed by the divinity,' without carnal wills and human thoughts, as the most holy Athanasius says. Yet he did not maintain that he, as man (for he is also God by nature), did not have a human and natural will, just as [he has] also the divine and paternal one. And he hints at the very same thing in what follows, asserting: 'He was conceived without sin by the Holy Spirit and of the holy, immaculate and ever-virgin Mother of God Mary, and was born of her according to the flesh without contagion.' He also adduces that divine Scripture makes mention of the flesh both in praise and in blame; not, God forbid, reminding [us] that the Lord's flesh is to be understood as other in nature and substance than ours, for he knew that it was assumed from our substance, that is, from the holy womb of the ever-virgin Mother of God, who is of one race with us, but [as] alien to vice, and in no way having, as we do, the law of transgression warring in the members against the law of the spirit. For, he says, no flesh corrupted by sin, which would war against the law of his mind, was assumed by the Saviour. For he whose sowing, which comes about through sin, the law of generation did not precede, has altogether no [such law] in his members either, but the law of divine justice shown to us as a pattern, which also utterly destroys that [law] which was brought in by the transgression of nature. For he came without sin to seek and save what had perished, that is, the nature of the human race, which had sinned. For there was no other law in his members, nor a different or opposed will in the Saviour. From this he shows, not that he did not have a human and natural will (for he does not appear to have said this), but that as man he neither has, according to the body, any operation through the members beyond the laws of nature, nor again, according to the soul, any contrary or irrational movement of the will, as we do, since he was also born above the law of human nature. And he proves more explicitly in what follows that his concern was only to exclude from the Saviour a vitiated and unnatural will, and that in the natural and human [will] he is indeed fitted to the paternal and divine one, but had no difference from it by way of opposition. And giving himself to us as a rule, what was properly his own he voluntarily subjected, while he commended the paternal [will]; so that we too, imitating [him], having rejected what is ours, may fulfil with all zeal what is divine, saying thus: 'For although it is written: I came not to do my own will, but [the will] of the Father who sent me (John 6), and, Not what I will, but what you [will], Father, these are not [words] of a different will, that is, a contrary and opposing one, but of the dispensation of the assumed humanity, which in compassion made its own the things that are ours. For he said these things for our sake, to whom as teacher he gave an example of piety, so that we may follow in his footsteps, and that each of us may prefer in all things not his own will but rather the Lord's.' So, as I said, he does not make away with the natural and human will, but with the vicious one and that which is beyond nature; and he testifies that we should confess that the whole [God] is free from all sin, who for our sake became incarnate in our manner. And, to put it briefly, by 'one will' I conjecture that he indicates that the divine will alone preceded his birth according to the flesh. And by what he says, that there is no difference of will in him, he maintains that he has nothing contrary or opposing, but [a will] in harmony and altogether wholly united. Hence, when he says that our nature was assumed by the will of the divinity, he makes mention of one [will]. But that which he introduces, 'I came not to do my will', he places the word in the middle [perhaps read: he sets the word forth in the middle] with number omitted. 'These are not', he says, '[words] of a different will, that is, a contrary and adverse one.' From which it is clearly gathered that two wills according to nature exist in the Saviour. For if he did not have a contrary [will], he had a natural one, as man. For what is not contrary is certainly natural, and no one denies it. For nothing in nature, or in the things that are according to nature, is at all contrary. (It is therefore a fearful thing to suppose what is not properly written in his words, and for the opponents to have contrived to make the letters of that man a cover for their own opinion, as not a good one, reporting these falsely in both respects, contrary to his intention. For he has as advocate the word of reason, which drives off every assault of the slanderer. And I indeed think that his sense is thus, cleared of every suspicion. And the most holy priest made me more certain of this, namely the lord Anastasius the abbot, returned from elder Rome, a truly incomparable man, adorned with divine virtue and prudence; who asserted that he had raised much discussion with the most holy men of that great Church on account of the letter which had been written by him to Sergius, enquiring for what reason, or in what way, 'one will' had been inserted in it; and he found them hesitant on this, and [yet] giving an account. Moreover, also he who composed it in Latin words at his command, namely the lord abbot John, the most holy *symponus* [secretary], affirmed that he had in no way made mention in it, by number, of one will in every respect, although this has now been invented by those who translated it into the Greek tongue; nor indeed [did he mean] any emptying or abolition of the natural will of the Saviour according to his humanity, but the complete casting down and destruction of that which is ours and has become reprobate, according to which war is waged even between things that are of one kind. [He was] wishing to show that the assumed flesh was pure of all sin, according to the tradition of the most sacred oracles and of the fathers' teachings. And it is evident how such statements agree with those which have just been recited by my lowliness, and have become, as it were, witnesses to the defence made for Honorius. When he had answered these things by reasoning, I marvelled, recognising fully their subtlety, and was in a way astounded at the cunning of those who impiously dare to do everything in vain for the sake of 'one', and wish, as has been their custom of old and is now, by stealthy and false tales to draw to themselves, in such a way and indeed without any reason, those who contend magnanimously against them, and to falsify a sense that in no way follows them. Having learned this too, then, as necessary, I have made it known to you, lord, honourable father, so that, fortified in every respect, you may know how to pursue the phalanxes of the adversaries, striking with the word tirelessly and overcoming mightily by faith, and having from this the glory of the Only-begotten for [your] proclamation, and as diadem communion with him through grace and union.
II.
EXTRACT FROM THE LETTER OF SAINT MAXIMUS TO PETER THE ILLUSTRIOUS.
He mentions Pyrrhus, and Saint Sophronius bishop of Jerusalem, and Pope Honorius, continuing thus after some [other] matters.
(Mansi, Conc. Collect., vol. X.)

By your praiseworthy letters you deigned to inform your unworthy servant about the abbot Pyrrhus. And after a little: And it would certainly have come about that, perhaps for this cause, for the refutation of him and of all who follow the impious novelty after him, I would without hesitation have hastened to your footsteps, to be divinely preserved and most renowned, so that all who like you are lovers of piety might know, together with their utter ignorance, also the superfluous abundance of their impiety. But I feared that I might be thought to be doing something outside the sacred laws, doing this against the will of the most holy see of the apostolic men, who lead well the whole fullness of the catholic Church, and guide it in order according to the divine law. For by this divine law, clearly, things heavenly and earthly stand, and one must in no way swerve from it; rather those who have resolved to live holily, as you do, must do divine things according to God, so that they may have God as the overseer of their deeds, and a reception without [mis]success. For, most renowned lord, worse than those, as I also intimated before, is the new faith and exposition, [worse] even than [that of] the ancient heretics. For this, through the many years for which he lasted in the episcopate, to the manifestation of his reprobate mind (for God knows often to bear patiently even for the disclosure of wickedness, not to make it greater by the delay, but to punish it more justly when it has grown greater), his predecessor impiously nourished in the womb, while this man more impiously gave birth to it, and again their successors cultivate it in contempt of the Godhead. And a little after: And what is a custom still worse than those, and as it were the special mark of all perverse heretics, is that they describe the innocent as guilty of their own impiety. For they whisper that Sophronius, who wisely taught divine things thoroughly and preached the dogmas of the catholic Church, moved them into error for this reason. And after a little: For the divine Sophronius, as you yourselves bear witness, most praiseworthy ones, was staying in the region of the Africans with me and with all the foreign monks, when they were contriving those perversities against all. And after a little: And the house of all was, through divine concord and unanimity, [joined] in one by the favour of God's grace throughout the whole world that lies under the sun, the Churches being fortified by a peaceful and tranquil faith. But those who envied their harmony and the confession of Christ God, like some murky cloud, or a roaring or heavy wave of the sea and of barbarians, with no one moving them but only the demon, friend of turmoil, who has stirred the human race to enmity, suddenly devised against the true faith of the Christians a new Ecthesis; then judgements in its favour and unjust compositions; then proceedings of records; then robber synods, and gatherings of bishops not convening by choice but assembled by violence, not hastening at exhortation but travelling abroad in flight from the barbarians; then commands and threats sent here and there against the pious. For they reduced him who was then emperor to servitude, sophistically, by gifts. And after a little: They persuaded the man to issue the Ecthesis in his own name. A little after: But he becomes their enemy and defender alike, or rather, it should be said, their supporter and accuser, publishing their argument and making known that he himself was in no way moved of himself, but, compelled by them, had made the most impious Ecthesis, saying this in writing on his own behalf, and giving account to John of holy memory, formerly pope of elder Rome. And after a little: And they convict themselves that they, the very valiant ones, quite manifestly made this, and by no means he. For he had no zeal at all about this, being taken up with other things. After a few [words]: Concerning all of which the wretches did not even have the mind of the apostolic see, and, what is most worthy of laughter, or rather, to speak more properly, of lament, as showing their audacity, they did not hesitate rashly to lie even against the apostolic see itself; but as if they had been made [sharers] of its counsel, and as though having received some decree from it, in their proceedings composed for the impious Ecthesis they took the great Honorius along with them, making a display of their presumption to others by the very great eminence of the man in the cause of piety. Who then, most renowned one, and what kind of Sophronius persuaded these false-speakers to do these things so atrociously and for so long a time? What church did not entreat them? What pious and orthodox prelate did not beseech them, crying out and adjuring, to cease from their own heresy? Indeed the holy Arcadius was breathing his last and giving up his spirit to God, yet even up to that hour he did not cease to entreat them. And after a little: And what [of] the divine Honorius, and what [of] the aged Severinus after him, what finally [of] him who came after this one, the holy John? Further, has he who now presides, the most blessed pope, omitted anything befitting supplication? Did not the whole East and West alike bring tears, laments, entreaties, petitions, both to God through prayers and to them through letters? But God indeed accepted the faith of these blessed men, and preserved a recompense for it unto the ages. They, however, despising the forbearance of the Lord, scorning those who kindly exhorted them to conversion, and remaining unmoved by the deeds of these eminent men through so long a time of supplication, would in no way suffer to prefer the heavenly faith to their own. After some [lines]: So the divine and great Sophronius, coming then to Alexandria, at once upon the first reading (for Cyrus had given him too those nine chapters of impiety to examine), crying out something mournful and loud, poured forth fountains of tears, fervently beseeching him, supplicating, pleading, prostrate on the pavement at his feet, that he should preach none of these things from the ambo against the catholic Church of God, since these were clearly the dogmas of the impious Apollinarius. And a little after: In such a way the men, O head reverend to me above all, tore at divine things with insults hateful to God and with, as it were, theatrical mockeries of one another, and in no way consoled the most sacred Sophronius, who lamented so piteously, as one bewailing the ruin of the catholic Church like a second Jeremiah, and deploring very well and most compassionately so great a fall of the divine dogmas. And after some [lines]: For if the Roman see knows Pyrrhus not only as reprobate but also as thinking wrongly and believing wrongly, it is surely evident that everyone who anathematises those who have rejected Pyrrhus anathematises the Roman see, that is, the catholic Church. For I omit to say that he certainly [anathematises] himself as well, being such, if indeed he is in communion with the Roman see and the catholic Church of God. I beseech you therefore, my blessed lord, to instruct everyone not to name Pyrrhus 'most holy' or 'gracious'. For the sacred rule does not permit him to be called any such thing. For he has fallen from all holiness who has of his own accord leapt out of the catholic Church. For it is not right that he be surnamed with any praise who long ago was condemned and cast out by the apostolic see of the city of Rome for the sense of an alien opinion, until he is received by it, converted to it, or rather to our Lord, through a pious confession and orthodox faith, by which he may receive sanctification and the holy title. Therefore, if he wishes neither to be nor to be called a heretic, let him not satisfy this person or that, for this is superfluous and irrational, since just as when one was scandalised by him all were scandalised, so too when one is satisfied all are without doubt satisfied. Let him hasten to satisfy the Roman see on behalf of all. For when it is satisfied, all everywhere will in common proclaim him pious and orthodox. For he speaks only in vain who thinks that people like me are to be persuaded and won over, and does not satisfy and implore the most blessed pope of the most holy Church of the Romans, that is, the apostolic see, which from the incarnate Word of God himself, and also from all the holy synods, according to the sacred canons and definitions, has received and holds, over all the holy Churches of God in the whole world, in all things and through all things, the rule, the authority and the power of binding and loosing. For with it the Word, who rules the heavenly powers, binds and looses also in heaven. For if he thinks others should be satisfied and does not implore the most blessed Roman pope, he does something like a man who is perhaps charged with murder or some other crime, and does not hasten to show himself innocent to him who by the laws has been allotted the right of judging, but only uselessly and without profit busies himself to show the purity of his conduct to others, private persons, who have no power to release him from the charge. Wherefore, my blessed lord, extend still further the instruction which is known to have seemed good to you and according to the good pleasure of God, that he may have no licence to say anything or speak against [others] on the matter of dogma. But learn his will clearly, investigating more fully whether he is willing wholly to assent to the truth; and if he is eager to do this, and hastens to it according to reason, exhort him to make a suitable petition to the most blessed Roman pope, so that thus, through his divine instruction, the things concerning him may be ordered according to rule and most fittingly, to the glory of God and the praise of your sublimity.
III.

OBSERVATION OF PHILIPPE LABBE S.J. Nor indeed should the royal collector have omitted the letter of Anastasius, librarian of the apostolic see, to John, deacon of the city of Rome, which was placed in the manner of a preface at the beginning of the collections edited by Sirmond. In it he not only explains the plan of the work he had undertaken, but also contains a defence of Pope Honorius against the censure of the sixth synod, by which he seemed to be included among the Monothelites, as Sirmond shows. Receive it, then, in a few words, as altogether necessary both for the matters set out a little before concerning Honorius and for those that will follow in the next volume.
LETTER OF ANASTASIUS, LIBRARIAN OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, TO JOHN THE DEACON.
To his dearest brother John, worthy Levite of Christ, Anastasius, the least, [sends] greeting in the Lord.

I had promised your diligence, since you are about to write an ecclesiastical history for the instruction of many, that I would translate certain things for you from the Greek tongue into Latin speech. For you had said, and with the fullest truth as your teacher had declared, that you could not confidently begin an ecclesiastical history unless some written series of events in both languages had come to your knowledge. Wherefore, since I recognise that I am so unskilled that I am not able to penetrate the force even of my own language, in which I was born, not to say of a foreign one, and for that reason would never have presumed to take up the attempt at translating in any way, yet consenting rather to be censured by masters than to keep you, through my sluggishness, from weaving the aforesaid history, see, I have made haste to satisfy you as far as my strength allows, fully trusting that whatever of mine is found crooked will be corrected by you, and whatever unpolished will be polished. Indeed I confess, with my conscience bearing me witness, that I would prefer these and suchlike things to be done by others, fleeing not so much the labour as my knowledge, unskilled in every respect, if indeed it should be called knowledge and not rather ignorance; not knowing whether, saving the peace of your fraternity or your purpose of writing the history, I could have omitted these things; for you surely shine with such a light of wisdom that you seem to have set before me to try not something necessary but a rash flavour. Therefore, since obedience intervenes, let it suffice me to have gathered with a rustic sickle what was sown by others, and to have carried it across on a faithful shoulder to the threshing-floor of Latinity, adding or taking away nothing at all. It will be yours, however, by adding statements, to enlarge the work of history as though with a winnowing-fan of judgement, and to cleanse like grain our words which you decide to insert into it. But we have undertaken the task of translating both these and other things in such a way that we may be known not to have departed in every respect from the very arrangement of the words, and yet may not seem, as far as we are able, to have fallen away from the truth of the sense. Further, I have translated certain short works of the most recent times, since those before us, or rather our elders, in translating the deeds of earlier times, anticipated us in a work of this kind, just as they also far surpassed us in excellence. So, after the Tripartite Chronography, which we translated at your urging, and certain other very brief works which we translated at the request of various fathers and brothers of ours, it happened that there came into our hands the apology of John the Fourth, Roman pontiff, for Pope Honorius, who was attacked by slanderers because he wrote [that there is] only one will of our Lord Jesus Christ. This apology, I think, renders him sufficiently excusable, although the holy sixth synod pronounced anathema on him as on a heretic, and pierced with the dart of reprobation one already placed under the judgement of God alone; since a heretic is produced not so much by the deception of error as by a wrong choice and contentious obstinacy. But who will there be to tell us meanwhile whether he himself certainly composed the letter from which the slanderers took the kindling for anathematising him, since such a thing could have happened either through the carelessness of the scribe or through hatred of the pontiff? although we are not unaware, since Saint Maximus teaches it in his letter which he wrote to Marinus the priest, that the most holy John the abbot wrote it. Suppose that he was himself the composer: who questioned him about it? who investigated his intention? who wished to correct him, and he resisted the one questioning him or trying to amend [him], or, serving contentions, pushed back? Especially since in that [passage of the] Gospel in which it is said: Do not judge and you will not be judged (Luke 4:17), and the rest, nothing else seems to the great and true masters of the Church to be commanded except that we should interpret in the better sense those deeds of which it is doubtful with what intention they are done. For there are certain intermediate deeds, of which we do not know with what intention they are done, since they can be done with a good and with a bad [intention], about which it is rash to judge, above all so as to condemn. In short, there are two cases in which we ought to beware of rash judgement: when it is uncertain with what intention something was done, or when it is uncertain what someone will become who now appears either bad or good. And how much rash judgement is to be guarded against the Lord shows openly, who speaks of the Sodomites in our manner, saying: I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know (Gen. 18:21). And again through Moses he says: Do not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling-block before the blind (Lev. 14). The Apostle urges this in almost the same words, saying: Each one of us will render account to God for himself. Let us therefore no longer judge one another, but rather judge this, that you do not place a stumbling-block or an offence before a brother (Rom. 13). And who is more to be called deaf or dumb than one who, when he lies lifeless and dissolved in the tomb, has neither an ear open to hear formally the charges, nor a mouth opened to refute the charges reasonably? But concerning judgements of this kind, what the venerable Anastasius, prelate of the apostolic see, teaches when writing to the emperor Anastasius, weighty with the authority of sacred Scripture, is sufficient. But lest we seem to accuse or rashly to reprove so holy and so reverend a synod, we think it permitted to us to hold concerning it what we know our holy fathers held concerning the great synod of Chalcedon. One of them, namely the holy Pope Gregory, indicated that it was to be received from this [see] only up to the setting forth of canons. And the blessed Pope Gelasius likewise, in his tome on the bond of anathema, intimates with clear examples and a number of divine testimonies how that same synod is to be received, where he concludes the treatment of these matters with this judgement: These and suchlike examples, he says, teach us, and divine testimonies confirm, not to accept indiscriminately all things said anywhere by anyone or written anywhere, but, keeping the good, to reject what is harmful. For the writings of the Greeks testify that this holy synod too promulgated certain canonical chapters, nearly all of which, however, since the apostolic see did not approve them, the whole Latin world has rejected. But why do we speak of this one alone, when the apostolic see does not admit even the second universal synod, which was first held at Constantinople, in the matter of the primacy of the Churches; and indeed decrees that all synods are to be received in the way in which the aforesaid Pope Gelasius describes that the synod of Chalcedon is to be admitted, namely for the communion of faith and the catholic and apostolic truth, for which the apostolic see delegated that it be held, and confirmed it when held? But if we wish to heap up everything that we can gather for the excuse of Pope Honorius, paper will fail us sooner than speech, and we shall surely turn our purpose of translating into the eloquence of composition. One thing, however, we will say, which beyond doubt we ought not to pass over in silence: that Honorius is such as he was declared to be; but if he was not such, he will surely not be the one against whom the sentence was set down, since, as it is written: Man sees the face, but God the heart,

But see, while our preface is being directed to you at too great length, we have gone far away from the task of translating, eager to show that on the rock of the apostolic see, as far as pertains to faith, there has never been found, not even through Honorius, a trace of the serpent, that is, of a poisonous sect. Take, then, the already mentioned apology of Pope John for Honorius; take also an apology for the same man, culled from the letter of Maximus, monk, and truly philosopher and martyr of Christ our God, sent to Marinus the priest. For the most blessed Maximus himself defends the already named Honorius not only in the aforesaid [letter], but also in the letter which he wrote to Thalassius the abbot. Moreover, in his dogmatic letter which he wrote to Peter the Illustrious, he calls him great and divine. From this letter, namely, see, we bring you certain things culled and translated concerning that same Pope Honorius and Sophronius of Jerusalem, of whom we have often made mention in the writings translated by us, and concerning Pyrrhus, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople.

Moreover, we have translated from the letter of the same Saint Maximus written to Marinus the priest a passage on the procession of the Holy Spirit, where he indicates that the Greeks bring charges against us in vain, since we do not call the Son the cause or principle of the Holy Spirit, as they suppose, but, not unaware of the unity of substance of the Father and the Son, we confess that, as he proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son, understanding procession, of course, as mission; interpreting piously, instructing those who know both languages towards peace, while he teaches both us and the Greeks that in one respect the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, and in another respect does not proceed, signifying the difficulty of expressing [something] from the idiom of one language into that of the other. For indeed by a pious interpretation of this kind Saint Athanasius once united the Easterners and Westerners who were at variance over the term 'subsistence' or 'person', when he taught them thoroughly that both believed in heart and held in understanding one and the same thing, although because of the difference of language they confessed it with the mouth in one way and another, and raged in untimely contentions. We have also translated, as the order required, certain letters of Pope Theodore, successor of the aforesaid Pope John, written to Paul the successor of Pyrrhus and to his consecrators; the style of the letters of these, namely John and Theodore, eminent prelates of the apostolic see, is redolent of Latin eloquence; from which it is clearly established that they were dictated not in Greek but in Latin. Hence it should be noted that the Latin world would have lamented certain things that were published in Latin as utterly buried under the weight of oblivion, had it not afterwards recovered them, drawn with thirsting breast from the spring of the Greeks' books, such as the letter of blessed Pope Felix pronouncing the sentence of condemnation against Peter of Antioch.

Indeed, just as also Clement himself, whom Rufinus, writing to Gaudentius, indicates was rendered into our language, restored, and returning, and clearly shows both that he had been written in Latin and lost, and received again. I have nevertheless excerpted, and see, I present to you translated, a certain narrative passage from the letter of Saint Maximus to the abbot, [telling] what the Roman legates did at Constantinople, for the sake of stirring up constancy in a cause of the greatest piety, for the refutation of the faint-hearted, and for the acknowledgment of the power of the apostolic see against those who strive to extort anything from it by violence. Further, see, I nevertheless set before you the acts of the exile of holy Pope Martin, which I had published at the request of the venerable Martin, bishop of Narni, together with the Hypomnesticum, which briefly sets out the acts of the saints Maximus the philosopher, and both Anastasiuses, and also Theodore, and Euprepius and others.
IV.
EPITAPH OF POPE HONORIUS I.
(Baronius, Annals, for the year 638.)
In the apse (which the illustrious pope made) these verses are read set round about, worked in mosaic beneath images woven in the same work, in a rough style (as the age allowed):

A golden picture rises from cut pieces of metal, and the day itself is likewise embraced and enclosed. You might believe, Dawn, that from snowy springs clouds rise, caught up, watering the fields with dew.
In the same half-circle of the apse the verses that follow are placed in a straight line:
Or such a light as the rainbow will bring forth among the stars,
and the purple peacock itself, gleaming with colour.
He who could set an end to night or light
drove chaos back from here, from the tombs of the martyrs.
What is seen by all turned upward at a single nod,
Bishop Honorius gave as dedicated votive offerings.
His features are marked out by his vestments and his works,
and he shines in appearance, bearing a shining heart.
